discovery: Quantum simulation of strongly correlated many-body physics with ultracold atoms in optical lattices

nominees.name: Immanuel Bloch
nominees.affiliation: Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics and Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Germany

nominees.name: Peter Zoller
nominees.affiliation: University of Innsbruck and IQOQI, Austrian Academy of Sciences, Austria

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / quantum many-body physics
motivation: In 1998 Jaksch, Zoller and colleagues predicted that ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise the Bose-Hubbard model, and that tuning the lattice depth would drive a superfluid-to-Mott-insulator quantum phase transition. In 2002 Greiner, Bloch and co-workers observed exactly this transition, turning a textbook model of condensed matter into a clean, tunable experiment. This established a new paradigm: atomic physics as a quantum simulator for problems that are hard to solve classically. Bloch's and Greiner's groups then developed quantum-gas microscopes with single-site resolution and single-atom detection. These made it possible to image Mott insulators, antiferromagnetic correlations, many-body localisation and entanglement directly. Zoller's theoretical programme with Cirac set out how such systems could be controlled and engineered. Together they built the theory and the experiments for a field that now connects AMO physics, condensed matter and quantum information. It shows the close link between theory and experiment that the prize should honour.
